utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Eoin Murphy, who is a graduate of Trinity College, Dublin, and will be attending Leiden University next year doing a masters in public international law. He's been with the team since February. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honour, before the start of the cross-examination, I wish to note that Mr. Mitchell and I, we will share the cross-examination responsibility. Mr. Mitchell will address the Srebrenica portion of the expert evidence, and I will deal with all other chapters of the expert report. And, Your Honour, when we asked for five hours of cross-examination time, we did this with the caveat that the outstanding decision of the Trial Chamber on the exclusion of parts of the report may have an impact on the time needed, and now that we have the decision, Mr. Mitchell and I are likely to need more than five hours that we requested in the beginning and that you allotted to us. We're not asking the Trial Chamber to make a decision until the moment it actually arrives, what we don't know, but I would like to foreshadow now that we have finalised our preparation and have now -- we believe that it may be more than five hours, rather in the -- in the period of six hours perhaps, but even if we very judicially and even if we attempt to narrow the scope of the cross as much as possible, but it is more likely that we will need something like six hours. We may well be requesting, therefore, some additional time in the course, but we will see how it goes. I just want to foreshadow this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, we have limited time. Therefore, I would kindly ask you to co-operate by giving short answers to the questions and very focused on the questions as such. Let me -- let me first turn to your CV that was admitted yesterday, and I just have a few additional points. In your capacity in relation to the Yugoslav Ministry of Defence position that you had, you also participated in sessions of the Supreme Defence Council in the years 1992 and 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended several sessions of the Supreme Defence Council, but I can't tell you exactly which ones. However, I was not a member. I was not a member even ex officio. I was occasionally invited to provide an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Dr. -- General, you accompanied Prime Minister Milan Panic on missions including a visit to Sarajevo in July-August 1992; is that correct? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. On that journey a US reporter, Mr. Kaplan, was killed. It was in August 1992. On that mission that escort of ours was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. -- or, rather, you prefer to be called General instead of doctor; right? That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was primarily a soldier, a general, and I appreciate that more than my doctorate but I don't mind whichever way you wish to address me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you toured the entire front lines during the event, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when I travelled with Prime Minister Panic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. I mean in relation -- in the time period in particular in Bosnia you toured the front lines not with Mr. Pantic but for other reasons; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time when front lines were active. Later on a study trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25278 on the screen, and as it is coming up, it is an interview you gave to the "Nin" magazine on the 22nd of April, 1994. You remember that you gave that interview, General, but --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave numberless interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now, we look at this year, and we look at the end of the very first paragraph. You say here: "I toured the Krajina. I was at every part of the front. I've been around the whole Bosnia, talked to people and have completely assured myself that this is an historic battle which the Serb people is fighting for its survival. If we miss this chance, we will not get another one like it ever again." I understood that you went through the area during the events, that means before you gave this interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I travelled on a study trip during that crisis, especially in Krajina, because there was a group that edited the magazine "Vojno Delo," was writing about Krajina, and I occasionally contributed to that magazine, and we made study trips to the Republic of Serbian Krajina while it existed, and on the way we also toured some front lines or parts of front lines that were along the way. After I was retired in 1993, I found a job at the institute for economic studies in Belgrade, and working to revitalise the military industry we toured Republika Srpska, and we also visited the Main Staff of the VRS. So I was able to familiarise myself with the situation at front lines in Bosnia-Herzegovina too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest that in Serbian we show the actual page. This is not that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It should be. Sorry, it is actually the first page, and it is -- I can't read the -- no. I see --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Trust me, this is interview with Oskar Kovac, who is an economist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, and it's "ekonomija."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then we have actually uploaded the wrong -- the wrong document, I'm sorry. In the English it's correct, but we have uploaded the wrong document. Thank you for alerting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we come back to this later on?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I can still ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you -- General, when you went through Bosnia-Herzegovina on these various visits, you came across devastated villages and settlements in Serb-controlled areas, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these devastated settlements would be Muslim or Croat villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also Serbian devastated villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there were the other kind, too, Muslim and Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And I just quoted to you something that you said, and unfortunately you cannot see the Serbian right now, but what you said is -- you speak of a historical chance for the Serbs that will not come again. General, the historical chances for the Serbs you speak about here, that was a state for all Serbs on all lands considered Serbian; right? That's what the historical chance was, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the basis of your objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, your suggestion to return to this when we have the original, and also from our experience with translations, we need to be cautious. We need to see the original too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have actually here a hard copy that we can put on the ELMO that will solve the situation because I don't know why it is so difficult to upload this. Here is the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have the first page. Please put the first page on the ELMO, and then we will use also a few other -- other ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, if you look -- if you look at the bit -- we need to see the end of the first paragraph. A bit -- now we can't see anything. We need to see the -- yes. So if we look at the -- you have to take away the paper. We need to see the -- yes, so if we look at the -- you have to take away the paper. We need to see the -- can you move the document a bit up, but we move the shadow. Yes. That's -- that's it. If you look at the last lines here in this first paragraph, it says: "I've toured Krajina. I was on every part of the front. I've been around the whole Bosnia, talked to people and have completely assured myself that this is a historical battle which the Serb people is fighting for its survival. If we miss this chance we will not get another one like it ever again." And my question to you was, General, the historical chance for the Serbs you speak about is the state for all the Serbs on all lands considered Serbian; right? That's what you meant?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant exactly what I said, for their survival. And "survival" means physical existence, saving your life. And once you've managed to save your life, then you see what you can do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the territory that the Serbs would need for surviving, that's defined by the six strategic goals, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I don't think anybody knew about those strategic goals except the people who discussed them. I didn't know anything about the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are talking about an article of the 22nd of April, 1994. By then you knew the six strategic goals, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know because I wasn't involved with this. I learned about the strategic goals only when I started working on this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: By working on this case you learned that -- what the six strategic goals were, and they were actually pursued by the Bosnian Serb leadership and also by General Mladic as commander of the VRS Main Staff. They all shared -- shared these six goals; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can suppose they were, but I wasn't involved in that, so I don't know. I don't know that first-hand. I learned about it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But by studying the documents you learned that, that they were all pursuing these goals?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The dispute between Karadzic and Mladic you referred to in paragraph 6 and 101 and 113 of your report was not about these war goals, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not a discussion of war goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The two at times had different views on whether certain concessions in negotiations were advisible in relation to the military strategy and the militarily -- military situation; correct? That's where they had different views at times; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the differences between them were not about that. There was no conceptual difference. The difference lay in the perception of the role in the system of strategic command, the decision to establish the army, appointed General Mladic commander, and starting with him down to the last soldier, everyone considered him the operative commander whereas the president of the republic --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. General, that is all discussed already in the examination-in-chief and also very rightly explained in your report. I would rather come to this a bit later. My question was very specific, and you have answered this. You mentioned yesterday during your testimony, and that is at page 41382, line 17 to 25, that the army is supposed to warn the Supreme Commander about the consequences of carrying out an order when they see danger in relation to the military position. That's right, yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he's the one who gave them that order. If the Supreme Commander gave them that order, and that has negative consequences. It would be natural to warn him. But if he didn't order it and they got their order from their own command, then, no, but he issued -- if he issued the order and that has negative consequences for the status of the troops or the army, then, yes, they would warn him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And -- and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript is catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, in line 7 on page 8, the witness said that all in the army considered that the supreme operative commander is General Mladic, and the answer as recorded is completely incorrect, incorrectly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it was incorrectly translated. And next one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is only with that answer. The last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript reflects that everyone considered him, being Mladic, the operative commander. I don't see any problem with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Supreme operative commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the answer after that beginning with line 17 on is not correctly recorded or interpreted. "[In English] But if he didn't warn them and they got the order ...," this is all -- "... the order and that has negative consequence for the status of the ... army ..." senseless. Witness said "if he ordered them" and not "warned them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, when I asked you about whether it would be the right thing to do for the -- for General Mladic to -- to warn the Supreme Commander that a certain order would endanger the position of the army, then he would have actually had the duty to do so; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if he got the order from Karadzic. But if Karadzic didn't give him that order, then he's not supposed to warn him. He needs to correct that decision himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when the Supreme Commander decided against the warning, to take it on board, then the VRS carried out the orders, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question really.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document is now uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes. Thank you. I didn't see that. Sorry. Yes. Now we can look at the electronic copy, because I want to continue now. The English has to be -- I think the English has to be slightly moved up. Yes. And the B/C/S is fine. Here in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you gave up your last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The question was actually answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said he didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, what I meant is if the Supreme Commander Mr. Karadzic had given an order and General Mladic would have advised and warned him against this order and opined that it would be harmful to the army, when Supreme Commander then decided that the order should be carried through the VRS acted and did that. They carried through with the order, did it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a hypothetical question. If you told me specifically what this is about, I would be able to answer, but now we can speak only in general terms, in hypothetical terms, and I'll give you a hypothetical answer. If Karadzic had ordered something to be done and that was not contrary to the rules of warfare, then that would need to be carried out, but if it's contrary to the doctrine and rules of warfare, then that must not be carried out. It's not carried out regardless of the consequences, personal consequences to the person who would refuse to carry it out, but this is like playing hide and seek. It's all hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much, but we have very limited time, so I'd rather want you to stop here. And as you are here as an expert, hypothetical questions and hypothetical answers are actually what is done. Here I would like you to look again at your interview, and on the same page, exactly the next paragraph after the one we spoke about, here you speak of the importance of Gorazde. You refer to the at least 70.000 people living there at the moment, the geostrategic importance for installing a Muslim state in what you refer to as former Bosnia-Herzegovina and you speak of the exceptional significance of Gorazde. That is one the most important points and it represents a natural link between Sandzak and Bosnia. General, Sandzak is an area in Serbia inhabited mostly by Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Serbia but Montenegro as well, because that's an area between Montenegro and Serbia. It is indeed populated by Muslims, but there's also a large number of Muslims and Serbs as well. To tell you the truth, I can't give you the exact demographic pictures, but there are entire villages and towns that are majority Serb and Montenegrin and, on the other hand, others that are majority Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we move one paragraph down a bit in both languages in relation to the significance of Gorazde for the Serbs, what you say is: "What is important for us is that the Muslims do not achieve this goal, that is the so-called Green Transversal be severed. It is important to us that the FRY border to what's the former Bosnia-Herzegovina be as secure as possible, and it will be more secure if this section of the border is in the possession of the, I hope, new Serb state." General, that was your view and also that of the Bosnian Serb leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a natural aspiration and desire. However, how much realistic it was is a different question. I know that in all maps that provided divisions Gorazde was never part of Republika Srpska. It was always in the Muslim part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, probably due to the geostrategic objectives that I mentioned here in this article.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The elimination of the Gorazde enclave was something you found reflected in the command documents, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elimination is a natural aspiration by anyone who is engaged in war and that is to control an area, but it is up to politicians to decide, and in this instance the politicians decided that this would not to be the case. The army wanted Gorazde to be within Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm coming to this. I'm actually showing the General now two orders. Your Honour, we will come back to this "Nin" article. Therefore, I will not ask to have it admitted right now but a bit later. Can we now please have Exhibit P00854 on the screen. It is an order dated 18 April 1994. And when you look at point 4 of this order, it says: "The president is ordering and kindly asking Hercegovina Corps commander to engage all available forces from TG Visegrad and to take over the part of the town on the right bank of the Drina River at any costs and push the enemy forces to the left bank by the above -mentioned dead-line before UNPROFOR -- before UNPROFOR forces enter the left bank, the left bank part of the town." General, the -- the Supreme Commander is here actively involved for the same -- is he actively involved, right, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot see what his order is from this. It only says that it has been ordered by him, but one cannot see the very order itself. It says here he is ordering and kindly asking. They two things cannot go together.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now please have P01645 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is an order coming from the TJ Visegrad command of 11th of April, 1994, regarding its participation in the attack on Gorazde, and under point 7 -- can we see point 7? Yes. Under point 7 is a message forwarded by General Mladic who visited the zone of combat operations on the 10th of April, 1994, saying: "Keep pushing energetically onwards. Pay no attention to what is going on around us. The Turks must disappear from these areas." General, you're aware of this document, are you not? You looked at command documents, so you have seen that before; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen a great deal of documents. At this point I can say that it looks familiar but I'm not sure whether I dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you look at the two documents that we just looked at, the Main Staff and the Supreme Commander, Mr. Karadzic, are actively involved for the same military result; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't see a document issued by Karadzic. Somebody's just making reference and at the same time ordering and kindly asking. If I were to see what Karadzic wrote, I could tell you more. The only thing I can say is to comment what I see written here. So this is not about an order issued by Karadzic, but, rather, one of the commanders is making a reference to it and at the same time ensuring an order and kind request, and this cannot go together. A commander can either order or kindly ask, but not the two at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I cannot show you this order because the Prosecution did not get all the orders that Mr. Karadzic submitted during the events, but the fact that the order is not here in front of us doesn't mean it doesn't exist, does it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost certain that it doesn't exist because there was no need at all for Karadzic to issue any order with regard to this situation, but, rather, there was a need for Karadzic to halt this operation because of the outcome that he considered to be the task of the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you also agree with me that orders can be issued orally; correct? Then there is a paper, except for a reference in a other command document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Commander doesn't issue verbal [Realtime transcript read in error "commercial"] orders. He issues all his orders in writing, and they are properly registered so that everybody knows what the Supreme Commander is ordering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 3. Oral.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oral orders. You said "oral orders" not "commercial orders"; right? Yes. Can we now please go back to the "Nin" article and that was 65 ter 25278, and we move now to page 5 in the English. Page 5 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, you speak here of the striving of the RS delegation to have a state and the power leaders of the world striving to prevent that by dividing Serb ethnic territory in former Bosnia-Herzegovina into enclaves that were not interconnected. And you are saying this in -- in -- at that point in time. That point in time, General, the RS territories were connected through corridors, were they not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were connected, but the corridor was constantly cut off. During my trips I often had to travel between salvos of fire, and it could easily be fired upon, and that happened very often and people were killed in this corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you also stated in your report at paragraph 10 that by the time the VRS was established, the strategic goals were achieved except for goal 6, the access to the sea; correct? So in May 1992, according to your words -- yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you further also state --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But on the 30th of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the date again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The interpreters could not follow you, so you would have to start again with "But on the 30th of May," and then they lost you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, the forces of eastern group Posavina where headquarters in Croatia occupied Movica -- Modrica and severed the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you devote an entire section of your report to the corridor connecting the Krajinas and other parts of the RS and the FRY, and that this operation started in May and was, in fact, successful at the end; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was successfully accomplished in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And a bit -- a bit further down you state in this article: "All those games," referring to the negotiations, "were eliminated by the wartime victories of the Serb people and its army." General, you were all in favour of achieving results on the battle-field and established facts on the ground; right? That's more helpful than, as you say, games during negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I didn't understand you correctly or maybe I didn't understand the question. This is a figure of speech. When I made reference to the games in negotiations, can offer you more or can offer you less, when they offered less and the Serbian side was dissatisfied, if they could eliminate these games through military victories then it was all right. That was my view. I'm not in favour of military victory as a option. I was championing a justified solution, and if you have an unjustified solution you have to resolve it through a military victory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If we look at the last bit in this article in the English and in the B/C/S you would have to look at the next column in -- on this page. When journalists ask you about the cities such as Brcko and Zvornik which were not predominantly Serb before the war you say the following, and now I quote: "The matter at hand is that it has to be acknowledged that a state cannot continue to exist if it has no essential prerequisites, and one of them is territorial connectedness of the entire entities populated by an ethnic majority. In the final demarcation too, an injustice will have certainly been done to different localities, but this can be balanced out through a certain exchange of territories." Giving what you said here about Brcko and Zvornik, your conclusion and arguments in paragraph 103 and 204 of your report that the Serbs took only the territory where they were in the majority is not correct; right? It doesn't apply to Zvornik. It doesn't apply to Brcko. It didn't apply to Foca either; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from this article, I said that there cannot be an absolutely justified solution. There is no absolute justice. There will always be a chunk of territory populated by another ethnic community that would suffer some kind of damage, and that can be rectified in a reasonable way by an exchange of territories, and you can see that I was in favour of a balanced solution. That the Serbs establish their entity only in the territories where they were a majority? That is true. However, there were some exceptions. But the key issue was that a territory must be a single and a unified one, without that there can be no entity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this article be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, to complete your CV in relation to military duties, you also functioned as the president of the prisoner exchange commission for the FRY in the years 1992 and 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my main duty. That was something that I did alongside my regular job. It was an ad hoc duty. But the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As the president of the exchange commission, you were aware that there were camps all over Bosnia-Herzegovina and civilians were detained and used in exchanges, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not within the scope of my responsibility, not Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was the chairman of the commission for exchange of prisoners between the JNA and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You received lists showing that women and children were among those detained and exchanged from Bosanski Samac, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25213 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, we have here prisoner exchange records for various areas, including Bosanski Samac, submitted by a certain Miroslav Tadic from July 1992. That's not here on the first page, but we need to look at page 5 in the English and page 9 in the B/C/S. At page 9 only very briefly. And then you see -- only very briefly on the bottom, on the bottom, please, in B/C/S page 9 on the bottom, and then we move over to page 10 in the B/C/S. Mr. Miroslav Tadic is a member of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac, according to this document, and sends records related to a prisoner exchange for the prisoner exchange commission of the Ministry of Defence in Yugoslavia speaking of hundred prisoners. And the president of the commission he's sending this to, that's you; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember that, but we didn't have any jurisdiction over Bosnia. They did exchanges on their own. My commission was involved in the exchange of prisoners between the JNA and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What it shows here is that you, General, forwarded this documentation that you received from Mr. Tadic to UNPROFOR. That's what it says here in this document. You remember that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. It was a long time ago. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now have page 3 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I point again to an error in interpretations, and it says -- actually in translation which says that we are forwarding this for your jurisdiction, whereas the jurisdiction was that of UNPROFOR. The translation says competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not an appropriate intervention. I can pick it up in his rewrite -- redirect. It is clear that I simply asked him that he forwarded it to UNPROFOR, and he basically says he doesn't remember that anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Karadzic should have understood it. Jurisdiction and competence does not make much difference. We can -- as long as we follow the flow of the evidence. I would like you to refrain from intervening. You understand I'm very -- I mean, the Chamber has been very lenient as far as translation is concerned. Yes, the Chamber is aware of the various issues regarding the interpretation and translation, but at the same time flow of evidence is also important. Shall we continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say just one word? The rest of the answer or the continuation of an answer during cross-examination can be adversely affected by errors of this nature. That's why interventions are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But take -- this example, the competence or jurisdiction, does not make much difference, Mr. Karadzic. I'm not sure if it is my English, but shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What you see here and we see here is a list of the Bosanski Samac commission for exchange of prisoners of war and detained civilians, and it is a list of 52 women to be exchanged; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have the -- the B/C/S has -- the lower part, please, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now, when you look at the names, it's all women; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we now have page 8 in the English and page 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we again have a list of detained women for exchange; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are Croatian words, but I suppose that the prisoners are of the Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says here -- don't we have page 8?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are Croatian officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Don't we have page 8 in the English and page 13 in the B/C/S? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these last names are Serbian ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does the stamp say?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The stamp is actually -- I'm looking at the lower -- the lower --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, if you do not speak to the microphone, the interpreters have difficulty understanding you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a stamp that bears the insignia of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina because there's a Croatian flag, although it's rather blurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have to move in the -- in the B/C/S one page further. I think there is obviously a mistake, because it should -- it should be a list from Republika Srpska, Serbian municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, let's find out what this document is about. Shall we hear the explanation of the witness about page 2. There are three stamps, one of which seems to be Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify something, Your Honour. This document, we left it in the original version how we got it, but it is a mix of documents coming from various areas, and I'm only talking about the Bosanski Samac ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But let's take a look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I'm may, I think it falls in the framework of 68 Rule, and we should have had it disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out the last part. Yes, we have English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but that is a document that does not relate to the materials sent by Mr. Tadic from the Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This 44-page document is just one document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was how we received it, as one document, but it's obviously a mix of various submissions, and the ones that we were -- that I am talking about with the General is just the few pages that relate to Bosanski Samac. And you can always see it by -- by the stamps on that particular page. We just discussed it in relation to page 3 in the English, and we discussed it in relation to page 8 in the English, and now we have -- so we should look at page 8 in the English and page 13 in the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is what I have here, all of these stamps are those of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could we then please have page 9 in the English and page 15 to 16 in the B/C/S. Page 15 to 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And here we have the Republika Srpska Serbian municipality of Samac, commission for exchange of prisoners and detained civilians, and we have here again a list of exchanges and -- so according to this document at least you saw on your desk materials relating to the exchange of prisoners of war and civilians and among them women; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember that. It wasn't my commission that was carrying out the exchange. There was just information to the effect that an exchange had taken place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone, and could all other microphones be switched off when he's speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you have to move a bit closer to the microphone so that the -- the interpreters can hear you better.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can these two -- these three pages that we've just discussed be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that only page 5 be admitted because the other pages which -- hasn't been demonstrated that they were forwarded to General Radinovic, so they're not relevant. All he sees is that in July 1992, there's an exchange proposed for 100 prisoners for 100 prisoners. Whether they're women or anything else isn't among the information that is provided him, and there is no evidence that any of those other pages of this compilation of documents were provided to him. So we would ask only that page 5 be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree with this interpretation, and that is actually a matter for the closing argument. What I had proposed to admit is the letter from the Bosanski Samac commission and then a few extra pages related to that letter of the Bosanski Samac exchange commission, and whether the -- the general saw it or not is then base -- is a matter of circumstance and argument rather than of admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the page where Mr. Radinovic's name appears.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Page 3 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I misspoke. Thank you very much. Yes. That's a letter -- that's a letter from the Bosanski Samac committee, and then we have underneath the -- this forwarding of the matters to UNPROFOR. So my proposal would be to admit page 5, page 3, and page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the letter that was sent to me in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Yes. That is page 9. Page 9, but only very -- at the very bottom, very bottom, a small reference and then the next page. The next page, yes. This is the rest of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd also like --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not my signature. This is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the date of the document, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The date of the document is --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The date of the document is unclear. It's only becoming clear from the Bosanski Samac lists that it's related to July and August 1992, and that would be the time of the corridor 92 operation, General; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But was he part of VJ army at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He was actually the president of the prisoner exchange commission of the Ministry of Defence of the Yugoslav Army. And we see here that his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was he posted in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were posted in Belgrade, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was in Belgrade then or whether I was in Geneva at the negotiations. I really don't know. But this is not my signature. I was not there. This information of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac is being forwarded with a view to facilitating this exchange, so that is not really within my purview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Somebody could have signed for you. Can you not see "za," "for"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it says president of the commission of the Ministry of Defence of the Army of Yugoslavia for exchange of prisoners didn't signed for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I see handwritten "for" in Serbian, "za." Shall we zoom in to the stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I see. It's covered by the stamp. I do apologise. But obviously I was not there at the time. I am not challenging that I held that position of the chairman of the commission. Obviously this was not within my purview, though, and that is why I'm sending this to UNPROFOR to get this done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will admit those three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also wanted to point out that page 9 and page 8 also relate to August of 1992, which is apparently not the same as what is being sent to him in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's still argument. It goes to weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you know that an expert has to provide truthful and objective evidence and should not be biased in any way with respect to the parties to the conflict in Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I speak as an expert absolutely, but as an author I can be partial, as a public figure, but not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: An expert should not misrepresent the facts to the Judges of the Tribunal even if he or she would very much resent the work of the Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not understand the question. I am trying to be as objective as I possibly can be and to the best of my ability and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I thought the question was simple. An expert should not misrepresent the facts to the Judges here, even if he or she would resent the work of this Tribunal. That was a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Actually, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it wasn't a question at all. It was a statement. Do you simply want the witness to agree with your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I want him simply to agree that an expert should not be biased against the work of this Tribunal, and I thought that was a question. That's at least -- but I move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you very much resent the work of the Tribunal, do you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why that would -- well, I have my position on everything, including this, but that is my personal view, my personal position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25279A on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is a speech you gave at the conference on legal and political aspects of the indictment of the ICTY against Dr. Vojislav Seselj held in Belgrade on the 23rd of June, 2005, and Mr. Seselj had actually published this in a book. You attended this conference; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on the first page the second paragraph in English and in B/C/S, the last bit, you were asked the question why Mr. Seselj was arrested and -- give the answer yourself -- were it simply because Seselj is a metaphor for Serb patriotism and the Serb identity. And a few lines further down in the English and in the B/C/S it's on the next page, you say: "I would just like to underline a few of my personal impressions on The Hague, that is The Hague Tribunal where I was misfortunate enough to have occasions to be several times trying to testify in defence of the Serbian generals. So further to what I believe must -- deeply and what I have learned. The Hague trouble is a powerful means of the West's extended aggression against our country." General, that's your view on the Tribunal; right? At least how you expressed it then.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my view to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this be -- please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This page?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, this excerpt. It's actually two pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- in the B/C/S, and -- yeah. Can we now please have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could we please have now 65 ter 25363A on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is an excerpt from your book, "Lies about the Sarajevo battle-field." You remember that you wrote this book, right, and it was published in 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: By then you had already testified in the Kunarac case and the Galic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we first look at the first paragraph in the foreword of the book, and you say here: "Can the Serbs accept without checking being named the guilty party for all the evils that have befallen these territories and these people in the last decade of the 20th century." And you say: "I can't accept this but I don't know about the rest." And a few lines further down you say: "These are precisely the motives that have steered the author in his ungrateful task to straighten a corrupt Drina." And a few lines further down in the English and it would be the next page in the B/C/S: "I was simply unable to bear all the knowledge I gained of the guilt of the Muslim side and the so-called international community for the destructive hate and obliteration that had occurred on both sides of the line of conflict on the Sarajevo battle-field." That's also your view today?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page in the English, please. The B/C/S is still the right -- the right one. And you say here: "I didn't call this book the way I did because I believed the Serbs are not to blame or because I believe that Sarajevo residents deserved the suffering by such destructive civil war or because I wanted to diminish the victims and the suffering." General, you agree with me that Sarajevo's residents suffered and that crimes were committed against them by the VRS? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree relatively, but it's not only the fault of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's also the fault of the BH Army that misused civilian buildings, civilian facilities. They did not protect civilians. They provoked operations from areas where civilians were, and in that way they contributed to the suffering of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we please move to page 3, the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes. Can we please have page 3, the last bit in English and page 4, middle in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Radinovic, you speak here of the partial confessions from frightened and blackmailed Serbian detainees at Scheveningen, and my question is: Is it your position that none the Serb accused that admitted their participation in crimes here before this Tribunal did so because they felt remorse? They were all blackmailed and threatened? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that is not my position. This is the position of an author who has the right to value an act as he perceives it at that point in time. At that point in time some confessions seemed like redemption to me rather than true -- an act of truly repenting. So had they done that, it wouldn't have -- it would have been better had they not done it in the first place rather than confess and repent.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 4 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you remember your book probably very well, and you have here a discussion on the use of the term "aggressor." And you say international factors but also The Hague investigators have fallen for the same lie even though they should not be entitled to such bias. And a few lines down you state in English and then continuing into page 4: "It is also only rational to assume that witnesses were coached how to testify by the Prosecutor and instructed to qualify the Serbian side as the aggressor," and so on and so forth. Is that your view, that the evidence collected by the ICTY Prosecutor was manipulated in this way?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly were manipulations. To this day I'm convinced of that, because an old lady who testifies says that she was hit by a sniper. How can she tell what the difference is between a sniper and an ordinary bullet from a rifle? She was instructed that it was a sniper. Nothing else would work, because it's not even easy for a military expert to tell the difference between a sniper bullet and a bullet that was fired from a regular rifle. And then "aggressor forces." How could she know what aggressor forces are? If you're listening to an ordinary person using language like that, "aggressor forces are over there, but not over here," that has to look like instrumentalisation. That is how it impressed me. And this is a book that is authored by me, and it is my right to write that way, and I am not equally proud of each and every part of my CV. You know, there are parts of one's biography that are emotional too. Some are rational, and then sometimes one exaggerates, but basically the fundamental views expressed in this book I wrote all hold. We can discuss the book on another occasion, not necessarily today only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, for a victim of a gunshot wound, it isn't really a difference being shot by a sniper rifle or by -- and a sniper of special training or a marksman, a good shot; right? For the victim, it doesn't make a difference; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter at all for the victim. That's not what I'm talking about. I'm saying that the victim was instructed to say that it was the result of sniper fire. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have full compassion for that victim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You are -- General, you are aware that people use all sorts of terminology in relation to people shooting from a far away distance; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the ordinary person would not be able to say what in military terminology and in relation to training sniper is. That means a highly-trained person; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an ordinary person cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But still they would use the term "sniper" in their everyday language, would they not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They say sniper shooters because they were instructed to say that. It would be more natural if they said they were hit by a bullet, not sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have the few pages admitted, please, of the book that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6449, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please, I'm sorry. I was waiting for this to finish. On page 32, line 12 it says, [In English] "... that I wrote adheres to all my fundamental values." [Interpretation] The witness said that everything that is written is based fundamentally on facts, not his fundamental values. Fundamental values.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Radinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, during your testimony yesterday and also in paragraph 38 of your report, you described the tasks you were given by the Defence, and you namely stated: "It was analysis of the control authority of Mr. Karadzic within the system of command and control of the VRS." That's your task; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then that is a question of bad translation. I said that I was supposed to analyse control responsibility of Radovan Karadzic in the role of Supreme Commander of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that yet again it is wrong. [In English] "Leading competence" would probably be more accurate. Again, it's "control responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going now into a debate about what terminology was right. I think we have his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we see there it's about the control authority of Mr. Karadzic in the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, that is what is written in the heading. That is the title in Serbian, but I don't know how it was translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I can -- I can simply read it again. The control authority of Dr. Radovan Karadzic in the strategic command system of the VRS. That was the task; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who gave you the task, any specific person?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got that task through the lawyer, Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you discuss the preparation of the report with the Defence team during various stages the progress of the report or only in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that first meeting we discussed that basic task, and after a while I asked to be given some time to study that task, to think about it, and to propose a conceptualisation of my own of my work on that report, and then I met up with Mr. Sladojevic. I cannot say exactly whether it was five, six, or seven days later. We talked about this, how I thought this should be done, how I perceived this task, whether that is what he thought was needed, he agreed in principle, and from them onwards we did not discuss this at all except for the fact that they sent me documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you receive all the documents that you used for your report by the Defence or did you do your own research in archives and through the materials from the Tribunal without their assistance?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents that are attained to this case I received from the Defence team, whereas some documents that I knew of and about which I had my own notes that pertained to the situation around Sarajevo -- well, I had some of them, I mean my notes. When I studied documents for the Galic trial, then I had some notes, and then I mentioned some sources, but I was absolutely certain that this existed in e-court, and I thought that it would be no problem to find that, that these were documents that were opted for in that trial. Which ones they were exactly I really cannot say at this moment. I would have to be reminded in order to say which documents these were exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you explain the repeated use of the word "we" and "our" throughout the report? And I refer here to just a few paragraphs. That's 15, 46, 64, 69. That's --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see the context. In published works, one often says "we" meaning the author. That's a convention in published work. I don't think it's used in other contexts. So could you tell me which --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It says -- when I read it I thought, Who is "we." When you say "we found," "we saw," I was wondering, did someone -- is -- do you have co-writers in relation to the report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's really the convention.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. Perhaps this is a point to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to address you on one particular issue. Page 33 today at line 11 to 23, Mr. Karadzic made an intervention in relation with the transcript, and you find it here and it says -- it relates to the transcript reference that I wrote here to "all my fundamental values." And then Mr. Karadzic said the witness said that everything that is written is based fundamentally on facts, not his fundamental values. I have been informed by a B/C/S speaker that that is not correct, that the witness had, in fact, spoken of his fundamental values and the word "fact" wasn't said at all. The fact that Dr. Radinovic ready agreed to this change is at least a very remarkable issue, and it needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But why do we have to discuss it in the absence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because I think he should not now be tainted even further. Because I wan to make two requests in relation to this. The first I would like an order by the Trial Chamber to the Registrar to compare the audiotape or video-tape with the transcript to verify whether the intervention of Mr. Karadzic was correct or not. And I think also for the rest of the -- this testimony, I would request that in case the witness doesn't speak English, he could simply take off the headphones and Mr. Karadzic could make his intervention in English or the witness would have to leave the room, because we cannot really check immediately now whether what I was told is correct or what Mr. Karadzic had said is correct. So I see no other way at the moment to proceed with these -- these new procedures in relation to transcript interventions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that the witness did not mention fundamental facts, but I explained that he said based on fundamental values general, not his own, and I noted that it means based on fundamental facts, not on his fundamental values.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it's not an appropriate intervention on your part, arguing that it's a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. One extra word was added, "my fundamental values."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be checked, and we will come back to this issue after having received the report from the CLSS. I will consult my colleagues with regard to the second issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.14 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. The Chamber is not restricting you to raise any issue in relation to the translation, but the Chamber urges you to be prudent and discreet in raising such -- making such interventions. With that said, we'll continue. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. I will do my best. And whenever it is possible I will ask not to be translated and address you in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, I can add this: It is improper to add your comment or supplement the witness's evidence by way of intervention regarding the translation. I take it you understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With regard to the portions referred to by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the Chamber still wishes to see the report from the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And please try your best to be able to finish in the originally allotted time. Do your best, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, do you agree with me that transparency of the expert's opinion in relation to facts, methodology and sources used is of great importance for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, as an expert when drawing your conclusions you would consider all material, weigh the value and credibility so that your report would be objective; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me that the quality of your opinion is only as good as the information upon which it is based?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also it depends on how well I know the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. When you came across -- first of all, did you come across information that contradicted your conclusions while you researched materials?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had come across documents that would be contrary to my basic evidence, I would quote it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In -- in preparation of your earlier report in relation to Sarajevo, you mention already that you had notes and that you reviewed the notes. These notes included interviews of members of the VRS that you yourself conducted; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, in fact, you confirmed in the Galic case that you interviewed 34 members of the VRS, including commanders and -- of the top level; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I turned over those notes to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you relied on those interviews in your Sarajevo report in the Galic case, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not too much, but I took them into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you incorporated portions of the Galic report into the Karadzic report; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly, but I did use that report, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you in preparation for this report here interview any members of the SRK since then?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And any other Defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you agree with me that it is important for transparency to proper reference the report so that the Trial Chamber can evaluate the credibility of your report or, rather, the credibility of the sources; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Krstic -- you may remember the Krstic Trial Chamber in front of whom you also testified discussed this with you, this particular point; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I suppose so. That's part of the discussion before any appearance before the Court, if you mean the credibility of sources, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But despite this guidance, you state in paragraph 54 that some of the author's views and arguments will often not be supported by relevant references because they form an accepted part of military doctrine and the doctrine of command and control. And I would like to address some examples. In paragraph 78 [Realtime transcript read in error "58"] you referred to the fact that before the 16th April 1992, that is the decision to set up the Serb TO, Mr. Karadzic had no authority over parts of the TO that were formed on the local level, and in paragraph 75 you refer to village guards basically being formed in local communes for Serb defence, and, General, you do not provide any reference for these acts; right? There's no reference in these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was common knowledge. I thought there was really no need for a reference in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it was actually not -- you did not research this early period because it was not really the task, included in the task, because that was about the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not relate to the VRS or the direct command authority of Dr. Karadzic, but in my earlier studies I got such information about the existence of those armed groups, parts of the disintegrated Territorial Defence, I learned that working on other cases. I knew that. It was just common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you know that Mr. Karadzic as president of the SDS had hierarchical structures of authority other than military chain of command but de facto authority; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no expertise in that line of work, but the SDS was the strongest party. It had won the elections, and it was the ruling party. It was in power. But he did not have the vertical of command, which is a prerequisite for him to have command competencies. The chain of command had not been established all the way until the army was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it may be minor, but in your previous question, in paragraph 58 General Radinovic stated Karadzic had no authority before 16th of April 1992 over the TO, but I couldn't find that passage in para 58.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I must have misspoken. I'm sorry. I said -- I meant to say 78. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you said --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I misspoke. It's in 78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you referred to 78 with respect to the latter part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's all 75.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Next is 75. That's about the village guards and how they were established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you have the passage that Karadzic had no authority over TO?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's in paragraph 78. Before the --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 78, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you meant 78 --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, not 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But there's reference -- oh, yes, in the latter part. Yes. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraph 81 of your report you explained the reasons why the Bosnian Serb Assembly appointed General Mladic as commander of the VRS Main Staff, and you concluded that the Assembly sought to limit Karadzic's control authority over the VRS. You do not provide any sources here for the reasoning in the Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cite the decision to establish the army from which we can see that his authority is limited, because the Main Staff was appointed and Mladic was appointed commander of the Main Staff, and that's how his authority was directly limited. The Main Staff did not remain the Main Staff organ but a command organ. By virtue of appointing Mladic commander of the Main Staff, Karadzic's role in the operative command the of the army was considerably limited. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraph 105 you claim that Karadzic believed that he should be on the top of the decision-making pyramid while Mladic and his generals thought that Mladic was the top person in military decision-making. That claim of yours is not supported any reference; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the nature of things the head of state is also Supreme Commander. At the same time, there is nobody above him in the hierarchy. Those are general points that need not be corroborated by any references. But when the Assembly appointed Mladic commander of the Main Staff, it disputed thereby that Karadzic was at the top of that pyramid. It introduced dual authority, dual powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You know -- General, do you know the book of General Milovanovic, "My view of the war in Bosnia in 1992 and 1995?"

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't read Milovanovic's book. I hope I will have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this book - and this book is, in fact, in front of this Trial Chamber as D825 - in this book at page 23 in both languages in the context of his criticism of Supreme Command, establishment of Supreme Command, General Milovanovic stated there could not have been no reason for such a decision apart from the excessive self-assurance of the inner circle of the RS political leadership convinced they could completely do anything. In practice, the peace of Josi [phoen] created a situation unique in the world in which the Main Staff could not be at the same time the Supreme Command staff. And in that same context he underlines it could be said that the Main Staff willingly obeyed the command staff anxious as it was to achieve the strategic objectives of the war and internal strife among Serbs. In this, we were successful. General, in the view of General Milosevic, who was in fact on the ground and contact -- in contact with the Supreme Commander Karadzic, the authority of the Supreme Commander was not at all limitless -- limited, at least as he says it. Would -- would he not know better than you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to take some time answering this. If this is in evidence, I should have received this exhibit. I don't know why I didn't. It's very hard to respond to such a serious matter off-the-cuff quickly, to answer your question. But if you put the direct question to me whether Milovanovic knows that better than I, then the answer was no, I was the one who taught Milovanovic how these things are done. I was his professor. There are, of course, examples when pupils outdo their teachers, and that's always nice to see, and I hope that's the case of Milovanovic. However, facts are relentless. Even Milovanovic is part of the group of generals who refused to obey Karadzic. So he showed, indeed, that what he says there is not right. Karadzic was not fully able to put his ideas into practice vis-a-vis the Main Staff. In the decision to establishment the army, it is stated that the Main Staff is the command of the army, not a staff organ. It was the operative command of the army. And in Karadzic' decision on the organisation of the army, it says the operative command over the army lies in the hands of the Main Staff. That's also written in the Law on the Army. There's no need for interpretation. These are explicit positions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness was speaking much too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
