utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all is recorded. The witness also said that it's not that they were undisciplined, it's that they understood their role in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness added at the same time: "That's also --" the witness needs to repeat this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of your overlap, the interpreters were not able to hear your -- your words as well as Mr. Karadzic's words. Please do not overlap. Please put a pause if you want to make a -- if you'd like to make any comment immediately following Mr. Karadzic's comment. But at this time we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 1 of your report you conclude that the VRS was effectively established on the 15 June 1992. Is it your position that until this date Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic had no command and control authority over the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was established on the 12th of May, 1992, under the decision of the Assembly, and on the 15th of June, Karadzic made his decision on the organisation and structure of the army, and he empowered the Main Staff to command the army. That means operative command in combat operations. Up to the 12th of May, he certainly did not have any control authority, because the army did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you yourself in the corridor operation, Corridor 92, and also this morning you mentioned that the VRS, despite having this command structure and paperwork, was already conducting operations in relation to the corridor; correct? So de facto it was already conducting operations, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Operation Corridor began in early June, not before. The forces that carried out Operation Corridor were in Western Slavonia, and only when the United Nations established UNPROFOR they started withdrawing, and from those units forces were made up for the Operation Corridor. That was in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we -- can we please have D428 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I assume you have seen this document. It is -- it are the minutes of the 4th -- of the 4th session of the RS extended War Presidency of 9 June 1992, and I assume you know this document because you reviewed minutes; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we see here that Generals Mladic and Gvero and Colonel Tolimir are reporting about the situation, and the Supreme Commander makes decisions on military matters, and that is before the date that you mentioned; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 9th of June, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You spoke about 15 of June.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the army was formed on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you said it was not operational until the 15th of June because there was no structure, but here we have actually the generals reporting to the Supreme Commander, at that time the Presidency of which Karadzic was a member, and then decisions are made. So that is before the date that you put it, 15th of June; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must have in mind the fact that the establishment of the army is not about one document in one day. It's a process. And the army did not start to be established before the 12th of May. There were armed units that would later become part of the army. Until then, there was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the 12th of May, the Army of Republika Srpska started to be established, and this process of formation was supported by the decision of the 15th of June prescribing its organisation, it's structure, et cetera, et cetera. But it started on the 12th of May, and normally on the 9th of June they are discussing the state of army, like a cross-section of the situation as of the 9th of June. On the 22nd of May, for instance, the 1st Krajina Corps was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, I was actually addressing the difficult situation on the ground. Between -- after the withdrawal of the JNA combat operation took place. It was the VRS that existed already, and despite the paperwork not yet matching the situation de facto they conducted operations. Is that not how it worked?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 12 of May, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was speaking about the situation between the 12 of May and the 15th of June. That was -- that is the period that I'm actually discussing with you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit D325 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, General, it is the analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the VRS for the year 1992. Are you aware of this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it is an important command document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a command document. It's an analysis of the situation. Based on that analysis of the situation, one discusses the good and bad sides. Measures are taken to address it. It is an important planning document, but not as important as it is taken to be in these processes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You did not refer to it at all in your footnotes; right? At least I didn't find any reference.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't mention it in my footnotes, because it doesn't address the issue of control authority of Mr. Karadzic, but I did say that Mr. Karadzic may have exert influence on the situation in the army concerning the combat readiness, but at various meetings or workshops, et cetera. This is what I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 7 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And paragraph -- if you look at paragraph 5 on this page, in the fourth paragraph, Chief of Staff General Milovanovic writes: "We carried out individual and concerted battle operations according to a single design and plan entrusting SUP [indiscernible] commands with details or overall missions as appropriate." General, that is how all armies do it; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And implementation of decisions of the Supreme Commander down to the military chain of command of the lower level, that is how it works; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it says here further: "During the past year the Army of Republika Srpska has been under a single command -- control and command structure despite the fact that initially we had a large number of different armies and paramilitary formations. General, there is no mentioning of any dual or parallel systems of command. It's not in here.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here he is speaking about operational command, so there is no mention of duality. They were indeed authorised to conduct operational control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is also a reference on -- can we please move to page 69 in the English and page 62 in the B/C/S. And in the fourth paragraph there is a reference to what the -- in the third paragraph is a reference to the Serb TO units established under the leadership of the SDS party. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that is basically also a de facto chain of command then; right? So the SDS channel.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it goes on to say as a form of self-organisation of the Serbian people for the purpose of defence from -- I think it says pro-fascist aspirations of the Ustasha and Muslim organisations and formations. So the issue here is the people who is being self-organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph there is a reference to what these early forces could achieve, and it says here: "They failed to achieve these strategic objectives of the armed struggle of the Serbian people in for former Bosnia-Herzegovina. They failed to open the corridors through the Sava river valley between the Krajina and the FRY or a corridor which would link Herzegovina," and so on and so forth. Sir, according to this document of the Main Staff of the VRS, the VRS did not just inherit what the previous troops had achieved as you state in your paragraph 10, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I'm saying and claiming is that the Army of Republika Srpska inherited the achievements of the JNA. It was the JNA who opened the corridor that was operational until the 13th of May when the eastern group of Posavina -- rather the Operational Group Posavina took possession of it and cut it off. But initially the corridor was established by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page is a reference to the withdrawal of the JNA as is said here, and I quote: "The pull-out of most of the combat hardware together with the personnel, the FRY nationals, was prevented." General, the VRS took over the hardware from the JNA and the soldiers from the JNA that were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These elements remained as members of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 152 and -- first 152 and then 153 in English, and then page 132, 133 in the B/C/S, one after the other as we move.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as this is coming up, these are concluding remarks of the Supreme Commander, Mr. Karadzic, on the 5th of April, 1993, regarding the previous year, and looking at paragraph 3, Mr. Karadzic refers here to combat operations involving offensive and defensive operations or concerted engagement of tactical units whose achievements have had results of operation and even strategical significance. You agree with this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask for the reference. Where can one confirm or find that these are actually my words, that it was I who said this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually if we look at a few pages further, you sign that document. You sign this particular document. Concluding remarks of the Supreme Commander. It's your signature. We can look at it at the end when we have dealt with the other references I want to address from this part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So, General, when you wrote in your conclusions, and I refer here to conclusions -- paragraphs 13, 201, 210, 211, 214 regarding the defensive character of operation, that is here, the Supreme Command, Mr. Karadzic, speaking of both, offensive and defensive operations; right? So your conclusions are not entirely correct, are they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusions are completely accurate. However, Mr. Karadzic is not familiar with these matters and he tends to call certain things operation which actually is not an operation. An operation means that it involves forces involving corps and other high-ranking units, and when he said operation, he probably had in mind an operation with tactical intentions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. This is a very complex issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, when you are using technical and professional language, it's very difficult for the interpreters to precisely follow. Could you speak more slowly, and kindly repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic used to speak about offensive operations, but he did not bear in mind that this type of actions and activities that he spoke about cannot be qualified as an operation. In the military doctrine, forms of combat operation are divided into operations, battles and struggles. The lowest -- lowest-ranking operations are conducted by lowest-ranking units and goes on in the same manner toward higher levels. And when Mr. Karadzic spoke about operations, he probably had in mind actions taken by lower-ranking units. Concept of defensive strategy can be composed of a series of small size tactical operations, and it basically can, despite of that remain as a defensive one. These are very technical issues and I hope you can follow me. I cannot make it more simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have actually addressed this also in your report, so we don't need to repeat it. Under point 4 Mr. Karadzic states that the Supreme Command as a whole, as well as every individuals member of the Supreme Command were informed of the objectives of planned operations and concerted battles and of their results frequently in great detail. So that is an important factor of the command authority - right? - to be informed and involved in the planning of such matters; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday during examination-in-chief, I said that Mr. Karadzic regularly received combat reports from the Main Staff briefing him about the progress of activities. I did not dispute that, and it goes without saying. But the point is that in the process of planning and conducting operations that are not strategic by nature, the Main Staff does not require an authorisation from the Supreme Commander. This is their inherent authority, and they can do it independently. They only have an obligation, and I mean the Main Staff, to inform him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic continues here to state that control and command of the VRS is united and that it is based on a high degree of concurrence and unity in selecting the targets of each individual operation or battle and in assigning tasks to individual operation and tactical formations. General, according to Mr. Karadzic there was a fully functioning command and control from the Supreme Commander down to the units on the ground, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not from the Supreme Commander. There was no chain of command from that level to the lowest ranking units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me refer you to the next -- to the next paragraph that makes it even clearer. Mr. Karadzic says here the relationship between the command structures and the organs of the government and the Supreme Command made it impossible for the Main Staff to make decisions absolutely on his own; rather, every operational battle was politically endorsed on the basis of the interests of the Serbian people and approved by the highest authority of Republika Srpska. General, the authority of the Supreme Commander is not diminished at all. He is functioning as the Supreme Commander and the army; the Main Staff is functioning as it should and as it does in other armies. Is that not what he's saying here?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he says here is that the army was functioning and God forbid that the army was dysfunctional. I never claimed that the army was not functional. We had remarkable commanders, and we had excellent officers who joined the VRS and they were fully capable of discharging their duties. But in the operational sense in terms of command they were not obligated to seek approval for their decisions. They planned them, they carried them out and only informed the superior organ. This is what I claimed. I never said that they were not doing their job properly or that they did not conduct the operations in an appropriate manner. All I wanted to try was to define the position and the place of Radovan Karadzic in the system of the strategic command of the army, and he retained his position as the highest ranking politician who is ensuring the government control over the army. This was basically my assertion. I never said they were doing their job badly. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have now page 154 in the English and page 134 in the B/C/S, and it is again a section of this combat readiness report signed by Mr. Karadzic, and what we have here is the setting of tasks for the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 155 in the English and 135 in the B/C/S, and then we have to turn over both.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We find here tasks for the various course detailed, and if you look at -- and you know this document, as you said, and the Judges know it and the party knows it. What we find here in this part of the combat readiness report are tasks that are in line with the six strategic objectives; right? Except for -- at least for the first five; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have P1388 displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's also mentioned in your -- sorry, no. That's a mistake. Sorry, ignore that. As it is coming up, it is the 39th RS Assembly session on the 24th and 25th of March, 1994, and you reviewed this document in preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 84 in the English, and it is 68 in the B/C/S so that we can see that Mr. Karadzic is speaking. It is the lowest in the B/C/S, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have Mr. Karadzic's contribution in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you then -- can we -- 68. Is that 68 in the B/C/S? Next page in both, please. Next page in both languages. And we -- at the bottom in English. We look at the bottom in English, and in the middle in the B/C/S. And Mr. Karadzic is saying here: I report to you and to the people, commanders report to me, the commander of the General Staff, GS, commanders of corps and brigades. And I established a Supreme Command so that I do not make decisions by myself. I did not establish it to use it as a cover. I'm the one who signs, who decides, and I will be responsible for each decision. That's reflecting effective control, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying that Karadzic had control over the army. All I'm disputing that he had operational control over the army. This is what I keep insisting on. The operational command over the army was within the jurisdiction of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I just read to you that Mr. Karadzic himself says that commanders of corps and brigades report to him. That's for -- much below the General Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Corps commanders, well, so far when reviewing the documents I never saw any report submitted to him by a corps. His reports came from the Main Staff, and that's the standard procedure. Although it is possible that it pertains to a significant situation, a corps or even a lower unit may send a report to him, but this is out of the ordinary. This happens only in exceptional circumstances, and I myself never came across such a report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was omitted from the transcript that lower-ranking units may send reports provided it is requested by the Supreme Command, and this is under the concept of exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please have P3039 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, as it is coming up, it is directive number 6, a document you are familiar with and that Mr. Karadzic signs as Supreme Commander on the 11th of November, 1993; correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And yesterday you -- during the testimony you highlighted the fact that the Chief of Staff drafted the directive that Mr. Karadzic signed. That is standard procedure, is it not, that someone in the Main Staff drafts directives for these command documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the chief of operational administration, not the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the -- this drafting is not only done for Mr. Karadzic. It was also done for General Mladic; right? He did not draft his directives that he signed either; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably it's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can, please, the word "drafting" be translated differently to the witness, not by using the word "writing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in light of the answer, he must have understood it. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Can we please have page 15 in the English and the last page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Reference is made under command and control to two command posts, including the one for the Supreme Commander in Pale. So in relation to this directive, there are two command posts with the Supreme Commander commanding the operation from Pale and the Main Staff executing whatever he decides in Han Pijesak; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any reference to an operation being executed by a Supreme Commander. A directive is a document of general nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also made a point of the fact that the two -- the two that they are not together in one command post would show that Mladic has more authority or basically is the one running the army. I'm just puzzled about this, because isn't it right that during wartime any corps locations of government bodies and commands should be avoided for safety and security reasons? Is that not the typical situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a typical situation. What we have here is the fact that the Supreme Commander is separated from the Main Staff command. In all armies across the world the staff organ and the commander are always at the same location because the staff organ provides support to the Supreme Commander in the process of preparing decisions. This is not the case here. In other words, it means that the Supreme Commander never prepared himself to draft decisions. Rather, it was done by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 4, to work on operational decisions. Not to draft but to take or make operational decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just a bit further down under point (a) is a reference to reporting giving the exact dates. That is a regular practice; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have no evidence to the contrary or documentation to the contrary it didn't happen with the Supreme Commander Mr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you have point (a) that I mean works in favour of my assertion. The decisions of corps commanders are to be submitted to the commander of the VRS Main Staff for approval seven days before a planned operation. You see that in point (a)?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but that is the normal practice, is it not, that the chain of command is -- his chain of command has different levels of decision-making?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approval is requested from the person who was supposed to grant it. Obviously in this situation it is the Main Staff, not the Supreme Commander, and that is why corps commanders are duty-bound when they're carrying out operations to submit their plans for approval to the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, not the Supreme Commander. I've been trying all the time to make that difference. I'm not saying that the Supreme Commander does not have any control and that he should not have any control and that he's not receiving information about what the army is doing, no, of course not. But operational command is in the hands of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you please speak a bit slower for the sake of the interpreters. And, General, I just noticed again you always speak about control when it comes to Mr. Karadzic. But he was not just the controller, he was the commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command and control and control is part of that function.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you mentioned in paragraph 102 that there was continuing disagreement between Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic and that Mr. Karadzic wanted to replace Mladic as early as 1993, and there's no reference for this. I would -- I would ask that -- I don't think we have to actually call up the -- this exhibit. You are aware -- are you aware that Mr. Karadzic promoted General Mladic on the 28th of June, 1994 - and that is in front of this Court as P3046 - and it is, in fact, an exceptional promotion? Do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not that this disagreement was there because Mladic didn't know what to do or because he was working poorly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you repeat the first sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason for him not to be promoted, because Mladic was a very capable and successful commander. Disagreement was not there because Mladic did things wrong. The disagreement was there because Mladic, on the basis of the decision on the establishment of the army, had this dualism, this dual authority within the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 261 and 280 of your report in relation to Sarajevo, you state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If there was no problem of so-called dualism, the operational control should have belonged to who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Operational control was in the hands of the commander of the Main Staff, but the president of the republic had the authority for the army to be used in accordance with a set strategic concept, that is to say to defend the territory of Republika Srpska and to carry out that concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me understand your observation about the dualism correctly. You said since Mladic as the commander of the Main Staff or commander of the VRS exercising his -- the operational control of the army, it caused the problem of dualism. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if such dualism would not have -- had not existed at all, who should exercise that operational control over the VRS, corps commander or Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Commander was supposed to have Supreme Command and control over the army, whereas in depth at all levels of decision-making others. The Main Staff was supposed to carry out staff and professional work for preparation and for army use. That is the definition for any staff organ, the Main Staff included; that is to say professional and staff matters to prepare the army and to plan its use, and these plans should be approved by the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I move now further to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraphs 261 and 280 of your report in relation to Sarajevo, you state that civilians and civilian buildings were not deliberately targeted by firing with the primary purpose of terrorising them and inflicting unnecessary suffering, but such firing with strikes on military targets. General, you studied the indictment against Mr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to the incidents charged in the indictment, the very incidents of shelling and sniping, you cannot state with any certainty what the circumstances at that moment were and whether the strikes were legitimate; right? That was not your expertise and the task; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my task but that is the conclusion I reached on the basis of the existence of numerous documents that I studied that show that the combat elements of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were deployed in civilian facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You know that Mr. Karadzic is charged with the shelling of a waterline of civilians in Dobrinja on 12 June 1993, killing 13 people and wounding 14, and that's a scheduled incident G5. There's evidence before this Court that the -- the victims were hit by 182-millimetre mortar round.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that is, Your Honour, in P1437. It's report at pages 8 to 9 and also in P1438.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You cannot point us to any specific source of evidence that fire was opened by the BiH forces from the immediate vicinity of this waterline at that point in time prompting the VRS to fire back; right? You cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't deal with that specific example. I assume you discussed that with that expert who provided that expertise. I just assert that it was a regular phenomenon for facilities and civilians to be misused for military purposes. Practically there was no need to target civilian targets because all of them had been turned into military facilities. That is my assertion. As for this specific case, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to this particular point, I want to direct you to paragraph 312 and footnote 198, and, General, in this paragraph you refer to a sniper platoon stationed in the Blagoje Parovic school. And I would like to have D3526 on the screen, and it is an order of the 1st Motorised Brigade of 2nd October 1993. And in -- it refers in point 3 not, as you say in your report, the Blagoje Parovic school, it refers to the former Blagoje Parovic school. In fact, this location was right on the front line. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. That's a civilian facility, a school, the Blagoje Parovic school. That is a civilian facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, a corps blockaded in a city as you referred to with very few original military installations would have to find facilities such as schools, factories, and the like and turn them into military facilities; right? They had no other choice.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they didn't have to be in town. Why were they in town? Why are they exposing the population to unnecessary casualties? Why don't they leave town?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just told you that this school or, rather, former school was on the front line, and isn't it logic that in the moment when the military take over a building and install their units in there, it ceased to be a civilian building. It's a military building, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is still a civilian building, but the military is misusing it and it becomes, thereby, a legitimate military target. The military is not supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, General, whether a given building is military or a civilian object depends on the use of this building, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Its primary use is that of a school, a civilian facility. The fact that it became a military object is misuse.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, yesterday at transcript page 41421, line 19, you explained your calculation of the number of military targets in Sarajevo, and you arrived at the number 2.200. In paragraphs 287 to 289 of your report, you arrive at the number of 2.000 legitimate military targets in the city of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you concluded that the whole of Sarajevo was one big military target; right? That's also there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Put in figurative terms, it is as if all of Sarajevo was a target.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpret's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you please speak closer to the microphone. It's difficult for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's put in figurative terms that it was all of Sarajevo. I don't think that all of Sarajevo was a target, but almost. If you take all of these localities all over town, it would be hard to draw that without all of it being a single colour when you're colouring military targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, your calculation that let you alive at number 2.200 as you said yesterday in the transcript and 2.000 as said in the report, you arrive at this figure in relation to -- on the basis of the number of brigades of the 1st Corps of the Bosnian Army as the starting point; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only on the basis of that but also on the basis of all other elements of the establishment of the 1st Corps of the BH Army and the strategic deployment of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their command posts, their Supreme Command post, Main Staff, workshops, military production, police forces. So it's not only brigades, but the brigades were the bases.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraph 51 and in footnote 151, you refer to a decision - and that is 1D1192 - to show how you arrived at the figure of 15 brigades. Can we please have 1D1192 on the screen just to confirm. If I count correctly, it's 13, not 15, in the first place, and it's only formed in August 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you do not know how many brigades were there before this date; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that date I don't know how many brigades were there, because we don't have information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before this Court is already a list of the 1st Corps command of the 30th of April, 1993, and that's D496. You referred to this document also in footnote 182, and that lists ten brigades. And there's also a document from the SRK command of the 20th January 1994 - and that is P5968 - and there on page 2 it speaks of 12 brigades. And we have another one before this Court - that's D292 - an attack order of the 1st Corps of the 11th June 1995, listing nine brigades. So would you agree with me that the number of brigades changed over time and was never at the level of 15 brigades? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you on the number of brigades changing and that they became bigger, but the number of targets did not change significantly. So that number of targets in any establishment, in any unit, it can be calculated approximately. I've already said that this is not exact arithmetic but it is approximate. Sometimes --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, looking at your Galic testimony about the number of legitimate military targets --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that is 65 ter 25415, transcript pages 20995 to 21001.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You arrive based on such calculation at the figure of 1.500 targets. Do you remember that you had in the Galic case that number?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have -- could we please have 65 ter 25363A. It is actually now a P number, but I forgot which one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's your book, your book on Sarajevo. And we need to have page 13 in the English and page 11 in the B/C/S. And here you again make such a calculation, and here you have 1.800 military targets. So that clearly shows that calculations based on theory do not match reality; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The calculations are approximate, not exact. Let me just illustrate this for you. A battery, for instance. A battery can be one military objective, but it also can be 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I'm just wondering how can it be that in a few years even actually from your report writing to giving testimony the numbers change from 1.500 to 2.200. How is that possible if there's any value in such a calculation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These calculations are not there for measuring something exactly. Rather, it is supposed to indicate the problem that there was a host of military targets within a settlement. The calculations are approximate. So the difference -- well, if we were to calculate it each and every time, we could have the number change because we would pay more attention to detail, to the actual establishment of a brigade. So the figures would vary. But none of these figures are inaccurate, incorrect. It just depends at the point of time when it was done. We also had the organisational establishment of the corps after Galic's term, and then there were a lot more elements for the corps and the Supreme Command in Sarajevo than during Galic's service because this group. Galic's term was over in August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please now have page 18 in the English and 16 in the B/C/S. And on this page and the six -- the six following pages, if you could scroll to them, please, Mr. Registrar, to just so that it is a list of altogether 222 legitimate military targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if I understood your evidence in Galic case properly, it's based on 24 military documents of the SRK and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a sample of documents on the basis of which --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you repeat the end of the sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a sample of documents from the entire compilation of documents in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the documents, the list is based on -- they're not all from the same day; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you cannot claim that these 222 targets existed throughout the time period this Trial Chamber is concerned with; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since documents do not bear the same date, you are right, but since these brigades were always in town, then one could say that I'm right too. These brigades did not change their location. They were there in Sarajevo. Sometimes they were within divisions, sometimes they were within groups, but they did not change their locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, if we look at the targets included, there are many targets which are temporary positions like observation posts, sniper positions, firing positions, machine-guns even; correct? You nod, but you have to say yes so it is on the record.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And highly mobile weapons frequently changed their positions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That means the existence of a sniper position or moving mortars on a truck at a certain location is only valid for a specific target list. It would -- for a specific date and not for the entire period; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they are going to reappear elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but if a sniper or a mortar moved to another location and it is mentioned in another of the documents that you review, it would be double counting of that one firing instrument, whatever it is, would it not? You would count it, got also [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would be right, only if it had to do with the organisation of the establishment of a single unit. However, I'm not doing that. I am working on the basis of documents of certain units. So if this sniper appears in location N, then some other day it's going to reappear elsewhere unless it had been destroyed. That was my logic. I don't know if I'm right, but that is the only way I could see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, the question whether you are allowed to fire on a military target is a question of whether at that point in time when you fire that particular building is, in fact, in use for military purposes, would it not be?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we now have page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Can we now turn to page 15 in English, first paragraph, and 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned -- you discussed with Mr. Karadzic yesterday the rules book in relation to 82-millimetre mortars, and we have already just a few minutes ago discussed a certain incident involving an 80-millimetre mortar. And if Mr. Karadzic needs a reference, it is at T41416. In the book you explain the following: The 82-millimetre mortar rule state that an enemy target can be neutralised 25 per cent. This is considered the lowest acceptable militarisation rate. If one fires 24 shells on each target, which is 96 shells per target for an average militarisation rate of 50 per cent. And for the 120-millimetre mortars it would be less. And it goes into very -- in many specifics, and you have already dealt with that yesterday. General, do you recall that you also explained these figures in the Galic trial, where you also speak about -- how many shells need to be fired?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that firing a single round would not serve any military purpose? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firing one single mortar projectile does have a military purpose. It's called observation fire, methodical fire that warns of danger and puts the enemy on notice so he takes steps. So such a thing exists as a single round of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, the single round that hit the people in the waterline, that cannot have had a military purpose. It was hitting people wanting to get water; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this question appropriate? We did not deal which this case which we challenge and no evidence has been led to prove that it was indeed so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all it is -- evidence was led. We have it in P1437, his report. I've already mentioned that. And also P1438, investigative file, and also I make a very particular point here, and it doesn't really matter whether it was charged or whether it was covered with evidence. That's in addition the fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the witness said he was not aware of that case. He's talking in general terms about doctrines. He does not know the details of the individual case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was asking about a specific incident. Can you answer the question, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know about this specific incident, because I didn't analyse it, and I don't know. But what was the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was actually putting to you that the shelling was a single round of a water line of civilians in Dobrinja on that particular day could not have had any military purpose, firing a single round on a ground of people.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely not sure that it was fired at a group of people. It would have been fired at an active military target, missing that target and hitting instead the column, the water line. Of course civilians should not be targeted. If that's what you're saying. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me move to one last topic in relation to Sarajevo. Control of forces. In paragraph 24 and 247 in your report, you state that the Sarajevo situation is such that it is impossible for Mr. Karadzic and the command officers at all levels to exercise effective control over the conduct and combat operations of their subordinate units and commands. General, the ability to control troops is not a geographical exercise, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not only defined by geography. It's defined by the situation on the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, the ability to control and command troops is first and foremost an existing system of command and control. Would you not agree to that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the SRK had such a control system in it; right? It was a professional officer, professional command system; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you also state in paragraph 17 of the report that the report does not confirm any wrongdoing in relation to the Sarajevo charges, but in any event, it would have been instances of insufficient control of the command on the ground. That means unauthorised activities of the ground troops? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that, but there was no possibility of effective control of the conduct of all the possible renegades on the battle-field, offenders. And I could explain more if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At this point in time I would rather move on, because we have very little time. I was just wondering about this, because as you have looked at the command documents in -- in this case, we have before this Trial Chamber several documents related to SRK command orders for the use of air-bombs. Do you remember having seen those?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the use of air-bombs were ordered by the SRK command and not by the local ground unit or brigade or whatsoever; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When researching the materials for your report, did you come across the evidence of Witness Pyers Tucker?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that is P4203, paragraph 37.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing something like this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker described a co-ordinated military attack on the 31st of October, 1992, by the VRS from the north and south of the centre of Sarajevo with the apparent objective of cutting the city into an eastern and western half. Such an observation and such an activity would not be an activity of a lower-level unit; right? It would come from the RSK command; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I forgot and I just remembered. I had -- I wanted to tender the additional pages from the book. I just -- I just remembered it. I didn't ask for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add those pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you have said, we should stick to the five hours. I will now hand over to Mr. Mitchell, but I still have a few topics like the six strategic objectives and a few matters related to incorrect citations, but I can do this if time allows after Mr. Mitchell has finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff and Mr. Robinson, about the book. I was told that we have dealt with almost 20 pages out of 23 pages, so we will admit them all in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, before we get to Srebrenica, just a couple of quick points about your testimony so far today. You've read the RS Law on the Army, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P2603 in e-court, page 24 in English and 17 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What you're about to see here, General, is chapter 11 of the Law on the Army, which is entitled "command." Now, you talked earlier today about dual authority. I just want you to take a look at Article 173 there, which says: "Command in the army shall be founded on principles of a unified command regarding uses of forces and means, single authority, obligations to enforce decisions, command and orders issued by superior officers." General, it's there in black and white. The command system in the VRS is based on unity of command; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you go down to just Article 174, just below that, you've talked a lot about the control authority of the president, and we see your report is about control authority. Article 174 says: "The president of the republic shall be commander-in-chief of the army. The president of the republic shall command the army in compliance with the constitution and the law." Just to be very clear, the Supreme Commander commands the army; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the Supreme Commander commands the army as the head of state, not as the operational commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's talk about Srebrenica, General. You've made a lot of factual assertions in your report which aren't supported by a citation, and I've just picked five examples which I want to ask you about right now. If you have a look at paragraph 320 of your report. This is Exhibit D3864, page 122 in the English and 140 in the B/C/S. You'll see there, General, you refer to a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and General Zivanovic that you say occurred on the 10th of July. Now, there's no citation there, but I want to show you the conversation that I believe you're referring to. If we could have P4484 in e-court. Now, General, you say this conversation took place on the 10th of July. The Prosecution's military expert Richard Butler testified at length about this conversation and established that it occurred on the 8th of July. Mr. Karadzic, who is one of the participants in the conversation, has also accepted in this trial that this took place on the 8th of July. So can we agree that that's just an error and this conversation actually happened on the 8th of July? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously it's a mistake, because the conversation took place before Karadzic allowed the entry into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you say at paragraph 320 of your report that President Karadzic during this conversation simply made inquiries without making any comments or issuing any instructions or orders. Now, you talk about this again at paragraph 348, and you say in the course of this conversation, Karadzic does not issue any orders. General, I can count at least six separate instructions or orders from President Karadzic in this conversation. He says the blue guys should be treated properly; that if General Zivanovic needed reinforcements he should call President Karadzic via the Main Staff; to have someone prepare instructions for the journalists; for General Zivanovic to tell Krle - that's General Krstic - that President Karadzic couldn't get to him right now, General Zivanovic needed to go ahead with his own forces. And then you'll see if we go over to the last page, crystal clear, an order from the president where he says: "All right, General. Full speed ahead. Tell Krstic to go full steam ahead." General, would you agree that paragraph 320 of your report, that's another mistake where you say that President Karadzic simply made inquiries without any comments or issuing any instructions or orders? That's a mistake; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a mistake. He didn't issue a single order in terms of employing the forces. He didn't say use this and that unit for this and that task. Carry out a new task, capture a new goal. He assessed the situation in general. There is not a single military order there that implies a new use of forces, different from the current one, different from what the corps commander had decided. And in that sense, I believe my report is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, your report doesn't say President Karadzic didn't issue a new -- a new order relating to a new goal. It just says he didn't make any comments or issue any instructions or orders. We can see he very clearly does issue instructions and orders in this conversation; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thing is he wasn't issuing new operational orders about the use of forces here. That's the essence, not whether he talked or whether he commented on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's go to the second example I want to ask you about at paragraph 370 of your report, and this is on page 140 in the English, 161 in the B/C/S. It's D3864. If you can just focus on point 4 in this paragraph. Have you found that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning vehicles. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. And you say that the operational order of the VRS Main Staff and the Drina Corps to obtain the means of transport for this operation was only issued on 12 July 1995, after the last meeting in the Fontana Hotel and the consent of the representatives. So just to clarify, your argument is that the removal of the Muslim population couldn't have been planned because the buses weren't ordered until after that last Hotel Fontana meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not maintaining that the population -- in fact, the evacuation couldn't have been planned because of the buses. The planning of the moving out of the population could not have been carried out because that was not the expected consequence of the operation that had been planned on the 2nd of July, 1995. That operation was of limited scope, and it could not have been expected that it would result in consequences based on which it would be necessary to move out the population. That was an operation geared at separating the enclaves, and it wasn't possible to expect the moving out of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I understand that, General, but your report here says the operational order was only issued after the last meeting at the Fontana Hotel; right? That's what your report says.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit P4533.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And while that's come up, General, you'd agree that the third meeting at Hotel Fontana happened at 10.00 on the 12th of July, 1995? I don't think there's any dispute about that? If you can just focus in on the stamp of this document which is General Zivanovic's order to get buses. You can see the time there is 8.35 in the morning which is before the third Hotel Fontana meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. The third meeting was planned with the idea of having authorised representatives come, and there were talks with the representatives of the Muslim population at previous meetings and the moving out was agreed, but General Mladic insisted on authorised representatives so that there shouldn't be talk later about the agreement being made with unauthorised people. That's this meeting schedule at 10.00. At 8.35 on at that day, it was known that there would be a moving out of population only approval was awaited from the authorised representatives of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But we can agree that paragraph 370 of your report is inaccurate where it says that the orders were only issued after the third Hotel Fontana meeting. We can agree that that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Well, it relates to the 12th. It's not a mistake. It's still the 12th at 8.35 or at 10.00. Those half -- those 30 minutes don't make any difference in terms of the fact that I'm explaining here that the evacuation could not have been planned. That hour and a half doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me take you to another example that I want to show you, paragraph 401. This is page 150 in English. It's 173 in the B/C/S. And we see you in paragraph 401 say that the testimony of foreign witnesses in this case has confirmed that all those captives, they're talking about prisoners captured on 12th and 13th of July regardless of when they were captured were first brought to the collection point at Bratunac. That's not right, is it General, that all captives were taken to Bratunac. You've forgotten the men who were executed at Kravica, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, we've said that of course those who were executed in Kravica did not come to Bratunac. The collection at Bratunac does not apply to the people who were executed at Kravica, because Kravica was in the evening of the 13th, whereas the collection in Bratunac was in the night between the 13th and the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we keep reading down that paragraph, we can see you say: "Miroslav Deronjic reported on 13 July 1995 that 2.000 of them were already gathered there." Who was Deronjic reporting to, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't remember this minute, whom he was reporting to, but normally he should be reporting to President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You can't remember as you sit here today that Miroslav Deronjic was reporting to President Karadzic about the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I can't remember that specific case, but in the nature of things he should be reporting to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Deronjic should be reporting to Karadzic in his role as civilian commissioner of Srebrenica. That's right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 408, General. That's page 153 in the English and 177 in the B/C/S. And here we see you say there's no reliable information or tangible evidence about who decided to move the prisoners of war from Bratunac to Zvornik. And then a few lines down you say President Radovan Karadzic ordered Deronjic to move the prisoners to the Batkovic camp. And we can see you cite to a document there, P -- it's actually P02994. If we can have that in e-court. Have a look at the document on the screen, General, that you've cited to. It doesn't say anything about moving the prisoners to Batkovic camp, does it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Batkovic camp, no, it doesn't speak about it, but the Batkovic camp was a well-known place as a camp for that part of the front line, and this is where the prisoners were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I understand that, General, but you've made a factual statement that President Radovan Karadzic ordered Deronjic to move the prisoners to the Batkovic camp, and you've cited to this document and this document says nothing the sort; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't exist in this document, but to put it simply, this is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But is it true that you cited document as a reference to your statement that Mr. Karadzic ordered Deronjic to move the prisoners to Batkovic camp? Have you seen that sentence and the footnote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I saw it in the report, and now when I'm looking at this order, I don't see that sentence there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly the point, your Excellency. In footnote it is P02944.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the second number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't follow you. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Radinovic is referring here to P02944, whereas the Prosecutor called up 2994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President, because what he's actually citing to is the order of the RS president on the establishment of the SJB in Srebrenica, which is P2994. I think you'll see P2944 is something completely different. It's a video. I think it's very clear that this was a typo, and it was P2994 that the General was intending to cite to which contains nothing about an order to go to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear from the text General Radinovic made reference to the order of Mr. Karadzic on the establishment of the SJB in Srebrenica. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. General, just one more. The fifth example I wanted you to take a look at, paragraph 389. It's page 146 in English and 168 in the B/C/S. You say in this paragraph: "We know that there were a few opportunistic killings in Potocari but that after some of the killings the perpetrators hid in the woods which speaks volumes about their fear of the VRS officers." First of all, General, who were the perpetrators that you were referring to here? Can you give us a unit, a name?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, can you give us any foundation for your statement that the perpetrators hid in the woods after those killings if you don't even know who the perpetrators are?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. During the trials before the court in Sarajevo, there's been reference to this and that's why I said it, but I have no specific knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's move on. I want to ask some questions about directive 7 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can have in e-court Exhibit P838. It's page 10 in English and 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must intervene. The witness should have been shown the second page of the previous document, item 4., from document P2994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think if Dr. Karadzic wants to readdress that on redirect, he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, General, you can see directive 7 in front of you on the screen and you're very familiar with the language: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica." And you say at paragraph 323 of your report that you don't wish to defend this sentence. The reason you don't want to defend this sentence is because it's an illegal order, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you agree that a specific reference to no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa means it's not only that those towns will be captured but the population's going to be moved out as well; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could expect that if the measures envisaged here were implemented. However, there were a number of mechanisms that could have prevented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me just read you what you said in the Krstic case on this point. And the question that was put to you from the Prosecutor was: "General you would agree with General Dannatt's assessment of this order when he stated in respect of this particular portion of the directive that we're discussing General Dannatt said I think what is intended here is that Srebrenica and Zepa should be captured and I assume that the reference to no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa meant that not only were the towns to be captured but the existing population shall be removed." And then you were asked: "So based on what you've just said you agree with that assessment of this particular portion of the directive? And your answer was: "Yes." So you agreed in the Krstic case that that language meant remove the existing population; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I have in e-court 65 ter number 18970.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You may not have seen this document before, General, so just take a moment and read it.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the covering letter from General Milovanovic. And I've seen it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And this document means when you see General Zivanovic's signature down at the bottom that the Drina Corps received directive 7; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I tender that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, in your testimony yesterday at transcript page 41393, you said that if a directive contained orders that amounted to a crime, all such features had to be discounted and dismissed in preparing operational documents based on that directive. I just want to show you one more document, Exhibit P3040, page 6 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S. And you'll see just under point number 2 the same language by planned and well-thought-out combat operations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show the witness what document this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we can go back to the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you can see, General, this is an order from the Drina Corps to all of its subordinate units entitled "Order for defence and active combat operations, operative number 7." If we can go to the very last page. Second last in English. You can see that's General Zivanovic's signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you can see that it's drafted by Colonel Milenko Lazic. Colonel Lazic was the Drina Corps Chief of Operations and training in 1995, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go back to page 6 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S. You can see the language there under point 2: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." So the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, has taken the illegal language from directive 7 and he sent it out to every single one of his subordinate units; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I must admit that I didn't have this document. I didn't have this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that might be a good place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I informed the parties by e-mail earlier, but because we have subpoenaed General Andric for tomorrow, we propose to interpose his testimony so that he would begin his testimony at 9.00, and we would interrupt the testimony of General Radinovic, and we would expect General Radinovic to continue his testimony at around 1.15 tomorrow hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Radinovic, have you been informed about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the circumstances, the Chamber will hear Mr. Andric's evidence tomorrow morning and continue with your evidence when his evidence is over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask something? Does that mean that it might happen that I am not finished tomorrow? That would be very unfavourable for me if that were to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, that's very likely. It depends upon how much time Mr. Karadzic is going to use as his redirect and how much it will take for Mr. Andric's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It seems like it will be unlikely that he would complete his evidence, General Radinovic would complete his evidence tomorrow, but perhaps through the Victims and Witnesses Section we can inquire and try to solve the problem. Perhaps if it's something very significant with respect to General Radinovic, we can try to complete his testimony and maybe General Andric can stay, but as I was under the impression that -- I wasn't aware that General Radinovic had a problem to stay until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. We were just going to suggest the same thing. Now that General Radinovic has raised that problem it seems like it would be prudent to -- to check whether or not, in fact, we can do what Mr. Robinson just suggested might be done, and that is complete the General's testimony and then move forward with Mr. Andric to be completed on Monday once he's appeared before the Court and acknowledged that the subpoena has been complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I endorse --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you make a decision, may I explain what my problem is? My wife is seriously ill, and I had difficulty leaving her this time. If there is any possibility for me to finish tomorrow, I would highly appreciate that, but if that cannot be accomplished, then I'll stay. What else can I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If General Andric's testimony could start later on -- later tomorrow, I would prefer to continue General Radinovic's evidence, but I will leave it to you, parties. So I will allow you to contact the witness, so for that purpose, and liaise with the victim and witness section. So please sort it out the best way in the interests of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of July, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.48 p.m.,
